prose.title: Real Deal Creel Traded for a Superstar, Then Paid Retail for the Rest
prose.dek: Keith Creelman traded for Puka Nacua, then spent {{f.team.0008.faa_spend}} at the Free Agent Auction, more on offense than anyone in the league. Real Deal Creel came out {{f.team.0008.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}: one superstar receiver and a supporting cast bought at the going rate.

paragraphs: Puka Nacua is an Elite WR1 and he is the whole receiving corps. The room ranks {{f.team.0008.wr_rank|ord}} in the league on his back, with Christian Watson at Mid WR3 next to him doing a passable impression of a starter. That is this roster in one line: one receiver only two other rosters can match, and a supporting cast bought at the going rate.

Quarterback came out playable, if not the fireworks the price implied. Dak Prescott grades Mid QB1 and Kyler Murray Mid QB2 — a real superflex pair with no passengers, and still only {{f.team.0008.qb_rank|ord}} in the league. Keith paid {{f.team.0008.top_buy_price}} for Prescott, which is a lot of money for a quarterback who grades in the middle of the starting tier, in a format where everyone needs two of them.

The backfield is better than it was and still only middling. Saquon Barkley at Mid RB1, Travis Etienne at Mid RB2, TreVeyon Henderson at Low-end RB3, ranking {{f.team.0008.rb_rank|ord}} — two real starters and a third body, in a format where most teams are guessing at the flex by Halloween. Dallas Goedert grades Low-end TE1, the last chair in the room rather than a hole, and the position ranks {{f.team.0008.te_rank|ord}}.

The defense is cheap by design: nobody on that side grades above the second tier, Gregory Rousseau and Jonas Sanker start at replacement level, and Keith put only {{f.team.0008.idp_auction_share}} of the largest auction budget in the league into defenders. He restocks off the wire instead — his {{f.team.0008.idp_adds_alltime}} defensive pickups are the most on record — and he dropped four defenders this week to make room for waiver claims.

In April he had {{f.team.0008.active_roster_opening}} active players and {{f.team.0008.cap_opening}} of salary on the books. Goedert was the only stud on hand, and {{f.team.0008.holes_opening}} priced offensive slots were holes: Deshaun Watson at quarterback, Henderson at Low-end RB3 as the best back, Christian Watson and Marvin Harrison Jr at Mid WR3, and three spots nobody on the board would rank. McMillan, at Mid WR2, was the one other piece worth starting. A to-do list, not a team.

The first real move came earlier that month, and it is easy to mistake for a footnote. He sent Kenneth Walker to HammerTime for their first-round pick. Walker was carrying {{f.team.0008.biggest_contract_traded_away}} a year — the largest annual contract Real Deal Creel moved this year — so the deal cleared that off the books and banked a first-rounder in the same stroke. That room is part of what he spent in July.

The rookie draft is where it got loud. He made three trades while it was running and used every pick he acquired. He sent the 1.04 to Gride, who took Jadarian Price with it, and got back Travis Etienne plus the 1.07 — which became KC Concepcion. He moved up in the second for De'Zhaun Stribling and up again in the third for Sonny Styles. Three trades, three picks, all spent before the draft was over.

By the time the Free Agent Auction opened he was at {{f.team.0008.active_roster_preauction}} active players and {{f.team.0008.cap_preauction}} of salary, and the talent on hand had more than doubled since April. Etienne, from the draft-night trade, was the best back at Mid RB2, and McMillan was gone for Nacua — Mid WR2 out, Elite WR1 in, one of the biggest single upgrades anyone made all offseason. The best quarterback on the roster was still Deshaun Watson, and the next body for the superflex spot was Michael Mayer, a tight end.

Then the auction, and he did not stop until there was nowhere left to put anyone: the roster closed at {{f.team.0008.active_roster_current}} active men against a maximum of {{f.league.roster_max_at_auction}}. Prescott became the quarterback, Murray filled the superflex spot, Barkley moved Etienne down to second back, and Henderson slid to flex beside Harrison. Studs went from {{f.team.0008.studs_opening}} in April to {{f.team.0008.studs_postauction}}, holes from {{f.team.0008.holes_opening}} to {{f.team.0008.holes_postauction}}, and over the auction window alone his starting offense made the third-biggest jump in the league. Committed cap has since reached {{f.team.0008.cap_current_spent}}, leaving {{f.team.0008.cap_current_room}}, which is loose change. Goedert, Christian Watson, Henderson and Harrison Jr are the only April holdovers left in his best offense, though Henderson opened Week One on the bench.

Two auctions, two months apart, and they are not the same event dressed differently. The Expired Rookie Auction sells players whose rookie deals ran out — men who did not earn a second contract — and only {{f.league.era_pool_size}} of them were sold league-wide. The most expensive one went for {{f.league.era_top_price}}, against {{f.league.faa_top_price}} for the priciest man in the Free Agent Auction. You do not build a team in May; you top up a bench.

Keith's May came to {{f.team.0008.era_spend}} for {{f.team.0008.era_lots_won}} players: Chris Rodriguez, Kayshon Boutte, Michael Mayer, Will McDonald, Kendre Miller. Rodriguez turned into a component of the Nacua trade, which is a decent return for what he paid. The rest are bench or gone, which is roughly what that pool produces for everybody.

The Free Agent Auction in late July is where the team came from: {{f.team.0008.faa_lots_won}} players for {{f.team.0008.faa_spend}}. Prescott alone took {{f.team.0008.top_buy_price}} — {{f.team.0008.top_buy_pct_of_spend}} of everything he spent there, and the most contested item he won all summer.

Nobody spent more on offense at the Free Agent Auction than his {{f.team.0008.faa_off_spend}}, and only C-Town Chivalry and CBP added more to their starting offense. For what the money bought, though, he ranks {{f.team.0008.faa_off_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}: dead average. With Deshaun Watson the best quarterback he had when the bidding opened, there was plenty to fix, and he paid the going price to fix it; Blake Bombers got the most for the money while spending about two-thirds as much.

He bought four quarterbacks there. Prescott and Murray start and both grade honestly. Jacoby Brissett, the cheapest of the quarterbacks he kept, grades Replacement-level QB and has not moved off the bench. Mac Jones was released in September. Buying a third and a fourth quarterback on top of a solved position is what happens when the auction is still open and you are bored.

The bottom of the market is where he is genuinely sharp. Cam Little, Tommy Townsend, Nick Bolton and Josh Hines-Allen all came cheap, which is the right way to fill slots ADP refuses to price. Parker Washington grades Mid WR3, the same as the two receivers starting beside Nacua, and opens the season on the bench. Same instinct as his waiver work: find the thing nobody is bidding on, take it, move on.

t.0008.faa_value.title: Who got the most for his money

captions.t.0008.faa_value: Ranked by how much each owner's starting offense improved between the auction lock and the close, for every dollar he spent on quarterbacks, backs, receivers and tight ends at the Free Agent Auction.

paragraphs: Keith made {{f.team.0008.contracts_count}} contract moves. Cam Little, Trey Benson, Brian Robinson, Charlie Kolar, Jack Strand, Jacob Saylors and Stefon Diggs all signed at the league minimum, and Diggs is the famous name in the set, though he grades Replacement-level WR and sits on the bench.

Chig Okonkwo is the one to argue about. He grades Replacement-level TE, he sits behind Goedert, and he signed above the minimum — but the deal is front-loaded, so most of its value is paid this season and the back years cost almost nothing. That is a defensible structure for a bet that has not landed yet: expensive now precisely so it stops being expensive later. Still a replacement-level tight end on a multi-year deal, though.

The Puka Nacua paperwork is easy to misread. Shawn Blake extended Nacua in May, before the trade. What Real Deal Creel did was cut Nacua's salary mid-auction — freeing {{f.team.0008.restructure_room_freed}} of bidding room at exactly the moment it was worth having — then put it straight back afterwards, ending on the salary and total value it started with. A maneuver, not a contract.

There were {{f.team.0008.trades_count}} trades and the three-way is the one people will talk about, because three-way trades are rare here. It is the only one ever completed through the league's own trade tool. He sent McMillan, his own first-rounder for next year, Chris Rodriguez and Omar Cooper, and got Nacua. It was not a two-team swap in a costume: C-Town Chivalry separately sent Drake London and {{f.team.0008.trade_blind_bid_elsewhere}} of blind-bid cash to Blake Bombers to make it balance. Three rosters, cash, and a pick, to land one receiver. He is also not short a first-rounder next year despite spending his own, because the Walker trade in April had already put HammerTime's in the drawer.
The last trade sent George Karlaftis, a startable defender, to the Hawks for a small upgrade in draft slot.

The rookie class runs to {{f.team.0008.rookie_picks_count}} picks. KC Concepcion came from the best slot of the group and, like De'Zhaun Stribling, grades Replacement-level WR so far. Omar Cooper Jr. was traded before playing a down. Sonny Styles and Zion Young are defenders who have yet to play a regular-season down, so the verdict on them waits for the season.

Start where it actually counts. Real Deal Creel sits {{f.team.0008.division_rank|ord}} of {{f.team.0008.division_size}} in Maddie Mondays, behind Sex Manther and ahead of L.A. Looks, and he plays each of them five times. Sex Manther is the better roster; L.A. Looks is the weaker one.

League-wide he is {{f.team.0008.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}. The offense has names at the top — Nacua is Elite WR1, Prescott Mid QB1, Barkley Mid RB1 — all of it assembled in a single offseason from a roster that in April was mostly a list of names.

The weakness is everything standing next to Nacua. Christian Watson, Harrison and Henderson all grade third-tier and are the {{f.team.0008.holes_today}} holes in his best offense, and with {{f.team.0008.cap_current_room}} of cap room, any fix will have to be cheap. The defense is thin too, but that is the cheapest problem in the league to fix. Trade for the star, pay the going rate for the rest: it is a real strategy, and it is one good receiver short of a division.

One last thing, and it is one night. {{f.league.wk_teams_final}} NFL teams had played when this was written and exactly one Real Deal Creel player was among them: TreVeyon Henderson, on the bench, who did not record a scoring stat. {{f.team.0008.wk_points_final}} points banked, because nothing he started has kicked off yet. Every argument above is still entirely untested, which is the only honest place to end.
